weekly_highlights.title: Indonesia's Current Account Deficit Widens Sharply to $12.5 Billion in Q2 2026
weekly_highlights.summary: Indonesia's current account deficit significantly widened to $12.5 billion in Q2 2026, up from $3.6 billion in Q1, reaching 3.3% of GDP. This deterioration was primarily driven by increased oil imports due to high global crude prices and a shrinking non-oil and gas trade surplus.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: A sharply widening current account deficit puts significant downward pressure on the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) and could deter foreign investment, impacting the IHSG and potentially leading to higher SBN yields as BI may need to intervene.

weekly_highlights.title: Gold Price Surges to Two-Month High Amid Dollar Weakness and Treasury Buybacks
weekly_highlights.summary: Gold prices reached $4,557.60, their highest since early June, following the US Treasury's announcement to double its liquidity support buyback operations for 10-to-30 year securities and a weakening US Dollar. Analysts note the combination of lower yields and a weaker dollar provided fresh tailwind for the precious metal.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: Increased US Treasury buybacks and a weakening dollar could lead to lower US yields, making Indonesian SBNs more attractive and potentially strengthening the IDR. Higher gold prices also provide a positive sentiment for commodity-exporting nations like Indonesia.

weekly_highlights.title: Brent Crude Nears $93 as Strait of Hormuz Standoff Continues
weekly_highlights.summary: Brent crude climbed toward $92–93 a barrel, extending gains for a fourth consecutive session, due to persistent uncertainty over the US and Iran reaching an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Oil shipments through the strait fell sharply to 4.9 million barrels per day in Q2 2026 from 21.6 million before the conflict.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: Rising Brent crude prices will increase Indonesia's oil import costs, potentially widening the current account deficit and putting pressure on the IDR. It also increases the burden on the government's fuel subsidy budget, potentially leading to higher domestic inflation.

weekly_highlights.title: Gold Experiences Major Bullish Breakout, Rallying 10% in August
weekly_highlights.summary: Gold (XAU/USD) staged a 10% rally from $3,942 at the end of June to $4,523 by August 19, with a 4.35% single-day gain on August 19, its largest since February. This surge is attributed to US Treasury bond buybacks fueling fiscal-dominance concerns and a shift in focus to US dollar purchasing-power risk.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: A significant gold rally and US Treasury actions can influence global risk sentiment and capital flows. A weaker USD and potentially lower US yields could support the IDR and attract foreign investment into Indonesian bonds.

weekly_highlights.title: Gold Jumps 9% as Fed Rate Hike Odds Fall Following Softer Inflation Data
weekly_highlights.summary: Spot gold rose 9% from $4,050 to $4,400-$4,420 as July inflation data cut the priced-in odds of a September Fed rate hike from 55% to 35%. Additionally, central banks recorded a record 288.9 tonnes of net gold purchases in Q2 2026, up 62% year-over-year.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: Reduced Fed rate hike expectations can ease pressure on the IDR and SBN yields, potentially attracting foreign capital. Higher gold prices also benefit Indonesia's commodity sector.

weekly_highlights.title: US Dollar Weakens as Bond Buyback Plan and Debt Concerns Emerge
weekly_highlights.summary: The dollar index traded around 98.8, on track to lose nearly 1% for the week, after the US Treasury Department announced larger debt buybacks. This move, aimed at containing borrowing costs, heightened market volatility and boosted demand for safe-haven assets, underscoring concerns over rising US government debt.
weekly_highlights.indonesia_impact: A weakening US Dollar can alleviate pressure on the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) and make Indonesian assets more attractive to foreign investors, potentially leading to capital inflows and supporting the IHSG.

major_headline.title: Indonesia's Current Account Deficit Widens Sharply to $12.5 Billion in Q2 2026
major_headline.summary: Indonesia's current account deficit significantly widened to $12.5 billion in the second quarter of 2026, equivalent to 3.3% of the country's GDP. This sharp increase from $3.6 billion in Q1 was primarily driven by higher oil imports amid elevated global crude prices and a narrowing non-oil and gas trade surplus.

key_insight.summary: This week's market dynamics present a complex picture for Indonesian investors, with global commodity price surges and US monetary policy shifts directly impacting the domestic economy. The sharp widening of Indonesia's current account deficit to $12.5 billion in Q2 2026, equivalent to 3.3% of GDP, is a critical concern, primarily driven by rising oil import costs due to the Brent crude rally towards $93 amid the Strait of Hormuz standoff. This deficit puts significant downward pressure on the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) and could deter foreign investment, potentially impacting the IHSG and leading to higher SBN yields as Bank Indonesia may need to intervene. Concurrently, a weakening US Dollar and reduced expectations for a Fed rate hike, following softer US inflation data and Treasury buybacks, have fueled a substantial 10% rally in gold prices. While a weaker USD and lower US yields could attract foreign capital into Indonesian SBNs and support the IDR, the benefits from higher gold prices for Indonesia's commodity sector might be overshadowed by the increased burden of oil import costs and fuel subsidies, exacerbating domestic inflation. Indonesian investors must navigate these conflicting forces, balancing potential capital inflows from a softer dollar against the domestic economic strain of a widening current account deficit and inflationary pressures.
